question: In early-stage venture capital, what does the portfolio math of a top-performing fund actually look like in practice?
guest: You know, probably a growth fund too, but in a venture fund we have about 45 to 55 shots, of which we need six to basically be a 10X or more. And we look historically at all of Sequoia's funds, and there's a high write-off rate. So when you say picking, are we actually that good at it? Our best fund is Venture 12, which includes Airbnb, Unity, and Dropbox. All three of them were billion-dollar gains, and there were also 10 companies that were $100 million gains. models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Top early-stage fund returns follow a power law, not a bell curve: one or two companies typically generate most of the fund's profits, and the rest barely matter.

In a typical strong seed or Series A fund of 25–40 companies, roughly half lose money or return less than invested capital, another third or so return modest multiples (1–5x) that roughly pay back the fund at best, and a small handful, often just one to three companies, return 10x or more. Data from Horsley Bridge (popularized by Andreessen Horowitz and Benedict Evans) showed about 6% of deals produced around 60% of total returns, while half of deals lost money.

Counterintuitively, the best funds don't have fewer losers; they often have more. What distinguishes them is the magnitude of their winners: a 3–5x+ net fund usually has at least one investment that alone returns the entire fund, often at 50–100x+.

The practical consequences: every investment must plausibly be able to return the fund, ownership and follow-on reserves in winners matter enormously, and strikeout rate is largely irrelevant.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
In practice, a top-performing early-stage venture fund delivers 3x to 5x+ net returns to limited partners, requiring roughly 4x to 6.5x gross returns to clear management fees and 20% carried interest. That outcome is driven by an extreme power law rather than a high batting average. Across a typical portfolio of 25 to 35 companies, even elite funds see 40% to 55% of investments lose money or go to zero, a loss rate surprisingly similar to average funds. Another 30% to 40% yield modest 1x to 4x exits that recoup only part of the capital.

Nearly all outperformance comes from one to three outliers (roughly 5% to 10% of deals) that generate 60% to 80% of total gains by each returning the entire fund or more on 20x to 100x+ deal multiples. To make this math work—say, turning a $2 billion exit into $100 million+ of proceeds for a $100 million fund—managers typically buy 10% to 15% initial ownership and reserve about half the fund for follow-ons to defend a 5% to 8% stake after dilution.

noweb.answer: In practice, top-performing early-stage venture funds run on an extreme power law rather than a high batting average. A typical $100 million seed or Series A fund backs 25 to 35 startups, putting roughly half its capital into initial checks for 10% to 20% ownership and reserving the rest for follow-ons in breakout winners. Across that portfolio, 50% to 65% of companies fail to return capital, while another 25% to 35% produce modest 1x to 5x outcomes that mostly offset losses and management fees. Roughly 80% of total gains therefore come from just one to three outliers returning 20x to 100x+ on invested capital. Hitting top-decile performance of 3x to 5x net to LPs requires $350 million to $600 million in gross proceeds. If dilution trims a 15% initial stake to 10% at exit, a $1 billion exit returns the entire $100 million fund once—meaning elite performance requires either a single multi-billion-dollar generational winner or several unicorn-scale exits.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A top early-stage fund looks like a lot of failure plus one or two huge winners. Returns follow a power law, not a bell curve.

Take a typical $100M seed or Series A fund that backs 25 to 40 companies. In a strong vintage, about half of those companies lose money or go to zero. About a third return between 1x and 3x. A handful return 10x or more. One or two "fund returners" each pay back the entire fund, and they usually produce well over half of total gains. Horsley Bridge's data shows that in the best funds, roughly 5–10% of deals generate about 60% or more of returns. Correlation Ventures found that about 65% of financings return less than 1x.

The counterintuitive part is that top funds often have loss rates as high as, or higher than, mediocre funds. What sets them apart is the size of their winners, not how often they're right. In practice, the top quartile clears about 3x net TVPI and the top decile about 5x or more. Getting there usually takes owning 10–20% of a company that exits for billions.

That's why VCs ask whether every deal could return the fund, and why reserves go heavily into the breakout companies.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: A top-performing early-stage venture fund is governed by a steep power law rather than a normal distribution. Consider a $100 million fund making roughly 30 initial investments. After management fees of about 2% annually over ten years, only around $80 million is actually invested into startups, with roughly half reserved for follow-on rounds. To reach top-decile performance of 3x to 5x net to limited partners after carried interest, the fund must generate roughly $350 million to $600 million in gross proceeds. In practice, about half of the portfolio will fail or return less than cost, another third will produce modest 1x to 3x exits that barely move the needle, and just one or two outliers will generate 60% to 80% of total value. Because ownership dilutes across later rounds, a single breakout winner typically needs to exit for $1 billion to $5 billion while the fund retains roughly a 10% stake. Early-stage venture is therefore a game of maximizing upside magnitude rather than minimizing failure rates.

A top-performing early-stage fund can lose money on half its companies and still return about 3× to its investors. The math usually hinges on one or two outsized exits.

Take a $100 million fund that invests $80 million across 20 companies and spends $20 million on fees and expenses. For simplicity, assume it puts $4 million into each company, including follow-on checks. Ten investments go to zero, six return 1×, three return 8×, and one returns 60×. That produces $360 million in proceeds, with $240 million coming from the biggest winner alone.

Assuming 20% carried interest on profits after investors get their $100 million back, investors receive $308 million, or 3.08× their contributed capital. That’s the cash multiple. The annualized return also depends on when investors put in their money and when they get it back.
